what: The tells — what makes copy, a voice, a picture, a clip or an edit read as machine-made, how to spot each one, and what a human maker would do instead. Every layer of this doctrine says what to make; this one says what gives it away. A tell is not a style choice: viewers punish work they read as AI-made, and the gap between how advertisers and consumers feel about it is widening.
added: 2026-10-13 — the owner: 'install deeper doctrines surround the emotional / visual / creative make up of our work because we are at the point of having full control of the content we make … so we completely eliminate AI sounding / looking generative output.'

source.rule: A row marked `research` names the work in `receipts` it rests on. Every other row is craft — observed practice in generated media and commercial production, marked `source: "craft"`.

why_it_matters.rule: Consumers already feel worse about AI-made ads than advertisers think, and the gap is growing; a tell costs trust before the message is heard.

master_rule: Generators drift to the AVERAGE — the average face, the average sentence, the average kitchen, the average camera move. Every tell is the average showing through. The fix is never 'make it look less AI'; it is always a SPECIFIC detail taken from something real: the swipe, the room's own words, a real reference photo, the brand's own footage. Specific reads as human. Average reads as machine.
hold_rule: A `hard` tell is caught by the machine with no model and is removed before the work moves on. A `judge` tell is read by a person or a judge prompt against this list and named with its id. Where the swipe itself does the thing — the source speaks in that phrase, shoots that way — it is the swipe's and stays: a tell is something WE added.

channels.name: Words
channels.what: The script, on-screen text and captions.

channels.name: Picture
channels.what: Every still: cast sheets, frames, plates.

channels.name: Edit and structure
channels.what: How the piece is cut and shaped.

channels.name: Concept
channels.what: The idea itself — the first, obvious, average idea.

tells.name: Machine vocabulary
tells.spot: Words generators reach for and people rarely say out loud.
tells.why: These words rose sharply in text after language models arrived; readers have learned to hear them as machine-made.
tells.fix: Say the plain thing the room would say. Quote the language bank.

tells.name: Ad-template phrases
tells.spot: Stock lines every generated ad reuses.
tells.why: A line the viewer has heard in a hundred ads tells them this is one more ad, and a generated one.
tells.fix: Replace with the swipe's own line shape filled from the bank, or cut it.

tells.name: Exclamation stacking
tells.spot: Two or more exclamation marks in a row, or more than one in a single line.
tells.why: Manufactured energy; people show excitement in the voice, not the punctuation.
tells.fix: Full stops. Let the delivery carry the energy.

tells.name: The tidy triple
tells.spot: Three parallel adjectives or clauses in a row — fast, easy and effective.
tells.why: Generators default to the rule of three; real speech is lopsided.
tells.fix: Keep the one that is true and specific. Drop the other two.

tells.name: The generic claim
tells.spot: A benefit that would fit any product in the category — 'feel your best', 'results you can see', 'made for you'.
tells.why: The average claim; it is the clearest sign nobody looked at this product or this customer.
tells.fix: The product file's specific fact, or the customer's own words about the specific moment.

tells.name: Over-explaining
tells.spot: A line that tells the viewer what they just saw or how to feel about it.
tells.why: Generators narrate; people let the picture land.
tells.fix: Cut the line. If the picture does not carry it, fix the picture.

tells.name: Even prosody
tells.spot: Every sentence the same pitch shape and speed, no breath, no restart, no filler.
tells.why: Real speech is uneven: it speeds up, trails off, restarts once.
tells.fix: The spoken slice's register recipe — fragments, one restart, fillers at the start of a thought — and the voice settings that allow variation.

tells.name: The announcer lift
tells.spot: The voice rises into a sell on the product name or the offer.
tells.why: Nobody talks to a friend like that; the lift says 'ad' before the words do.
tells.fix: Read the product line flat, the way the rest of the paragraph is read.

tells.name: Plastic skin
tells.spot: Skin with no pores, no texture, an even sheen; waxy or airbrushed.
tells.why: The commonest picture tell; generators smooth skin toward an average.
tells.fix: Real reference, the realism block (visible pores, fine lines, matte skin), the subject's own detail crops.

tells.name: The average face
tells.spot: A face that is perfectly symmetrical, flawless and forgettable — model-pretty with nothing particular about it.
tells.why: Generated faces drift toward the average face, which is why they read as trustworthy and anonymous at once.
tells.fix: Build from a real reference and keep its particulars — the asymmetry, the mark, the uneven brow.

tells.name: Studio light everywhere
tells.spot: Even, glowing, shadowless light in a place that would never have it — a bathroom lit like a product shoot.
tells.why: Generators light for beauty, not for the place; real rooms have one window and a bad ceiling light.
tells.fix: Light from the world block: where the window is, what the lamp does, the shadow it throws.

tells.name: The sterile room
tells.spot: A spotless, empty, catalogue room with nothing personal in it.
tells.why: The average room; real places have clutter, wear and someone's life in them.
tells.fix: The swipe's room inventory, sharper — the believable clutter, the worn surface.

tells.name: Dead centre, perfect pose
tells.spot: Subject centred, square to camera, smiling, holding the product up.
tells.why: The stock-photo pose; nobody holds a bottle beside their face in real life.
tells.fix: The swipe's framing and its real gesture — caught mid-action, off-centre where the source was.

tells.name: New-out-of-the-box wardrobe
tells.spot: Clothes with no creases, no wear, a perfect fit; hair with no stray strand.
tells.why: Generated clothes are ironed by default; real clothes have been worn.
tells.fix: Name the wear in the look: creases, a pushed-up sleeve, hair as it actually sits.

tells.name: The grade
tells.spot: Teal-and-orange, oversaturated, HDR glow, fake shallow focus on a phone shot.
tells.why: A 'cinematic' default laid over a format that was shot on a phone.
tells.fix: The camera block's realness dial — no cinematic grading — taken from the swipe.

tells.name: Broken detail
tells.spot: Wrong fingers or hands, garbled text, a label that changes, impossible reflections or shadows, jewellery melting into skin.
tells.why: The detail a viewer's eye catches in a second, and the one that ends trust in everything else.
tells.fix: Type is a layer, never generated; the product only from its real packshot; regenerate the frame, never ship it.

tells.name: The floating camera
tells.spot: A perfectly smooth, slow glide or push-in on a shot that should be handheld or locked off.
tells.why: The generator's default move; no phone and no person moves like that.
tells.fix: The swipe's own camera: handheld with its shake, or locked off and still.

tells.name: Slow drift and morph
tells.spot: Everything moving a little too slowly; faces, hands, products or backgrounds that shift shape across the clip.
tells.why: Temporal drift is the signature failure of generated video.
tells.fix: Shorter clips, first and last frame pinned, the product from its packshot; a morphing clip is remade, never shipped.

tells.name: Wrong physics
tells.spot: Liquid, cloth, hair or skin that moves wrong; contact with no weight; a gesture that never quite lands.
tells.why: The body knows physics before the mind does.
tells.fix: Beat-by-beat directions with the real action from the swipe's frame map.

tells.name: The dead stare
tells.spot: Unblinking eyes, a fixed smile, lip-sync drifting off the words, a background that does not move.
tells.why: Faces are what people read hardest; a still face in a moving clip is uncanny.
tells.fix: Line parity on every talking clip; a reaction beat on the face; motion QC names it.

tells.name: Metronome cuts
tells.spot: Every shot the same length; every scene the same shape.
tells.why: A machine cuts on a grid; an editor cuts on the feeling.
tells.fix: Cut to the emotional map: fast where the feeling builds, held where it lands.

tells.name: Too clean
tells.spot: No imperfection anywhere — no stumble, no off-frame moment, no real-world noise.
tells.why: Polish is the tell in a feed of phone footage; perfection reads as fake.
tells.fix: Keep the anti-perfection budget: the swipe's own roughness, carried on purpose.

tells.name: The music swell
tells.spot: Stock music that rises on the product reveal and resolves on the call to action.
tells.why: The template's emotional shortcut — the viewer hears the formula.
tells.fix: The swipe's sound: its own bed, its drop-outs, its silence.

tells.name: The first idea
tells.spot: The obvious version anyone would write first — the generic setting, the generic person, the generic problem.
tells.why: A generator's first answer is the average answer by construction.
tells.fix: Start from the swipe and the room, not from the category; change one thing on purpose.

tells.name: No specific human detail
tells.spot: Nothing in the piece that only this audience would recognise — no in-joke, no real habit, no particular object.
tells.why: Specific detail is the strongest signal a person made this for a person.
tells.fix: One detail from the culture read or the culture map, named with its receipt.

receipts.cite: Kobak, D., González-Márquez, R., Horvát, E.-Á. & Lause, J. (2024). Delving into ChatGPT usage in academic writing through excess vocabulary. arXiv:2406.07016.
receipts.what: Style words such as 'delves', 'showcasing' and 'underscores' rose far above their pre-LLM trend in 2024 abstracts — the vocabulary readers now hear as machine-made.

receipts.cite: Nightingale, S. J. & Farid, H. (2022). AI-synthesized faces are indistinguishable from real faces and more trustworthy. PNAS, 119(8).
receipts.what: Synthetic faces fooled viewers at chance and were rated more trustworthy; the authors suggest because they look more like average faces.

receipts.cite: IAB (2026). The AI Ad Gap Widens.
receipts.what: Consumers feel more negative about AI-generated ads than advertisers think, and the gap grew from 32 points in 2024 to 37 in 2026.
